description: XONIDU is an open-source development team from UNAM FES Cuautitlán, focused on software engineering, automation, and hardware, currently competing in the Challenge 13 Space Mission Design Game. We bring a proven track record, having secured 2nd place at the IA FESC 2026 Hackathon and 4th place at the Mobility and AI 2025 Hackathon. If you want to build a realistic, playable, and scientifically grounded space simulator, come join us.
summary: Xonidu is a space mission video game. You operate the Xonidu space station. You choose a mission, an orbit and a launch vehicle, and you manage limited resources while events threaten your mission. There are 9 missions, 5 orbits and 3 launch vehicles. In easy mode the events are simulated. In medium and hard mode they come from live NASA and NOAA data, like solar storms, flares and asteroids. Every decision changes your score.
details:
Xonidu Station is a first-person 2D mission design game. You pick one of 9 missions, then an orbit and a launch vehicle. The missions are satellite servicing, cargo capture with the robotic arm, EVA spacewalks, CubeSat deployment, microgravity science, Earth observation, Moon and Mars technology tests, satellite life extension, and astronomical observation. Your score starts at 100. A good orbit and launcher raise it, a bad choice lowers it. Finishing a mission gives points and data. A mission lasts 1 to 30 days on the station clock, and each day takes 1 to 3 real minutes depending on difficulty.

The station has six zones and 27 modules. Each module opens full screen. When a module is in warning or critical state, its zone blinks on the map. You have to open it and fix it before it gets worse. You have 120 seconds on easy, 80 on medium and 60 on hard. When a real NASA value gets close to its limit, the module warns you first, and you can reinforce it to buy more time.

The events come from live NASA and NOAA data, not from a script. Solar storms, flares, coronal mass ejections, solar wind, magnetic field changes, DSN antenna status and asteroids from NeoWs can all threaten your mission. Only recent events count.

To fix a module you finish a repair task on its screen: a keypad with live NASA values, a robot arm, a dial, cables, crew questions, a slider, a hold button, or an ordering task. Easy has 2 steps and no penalty. Medium has 3 steps. Hard has the full set.

Fuel is limited. Chemical propulsion has 200 kg and electric has 50 kg. Running out costs 20 points. A 30 day mission uses more fuel than the tanks hold, so long missions trade fuel against score.

The game runs on Render. One Python backend fetches the live data and caches it for 10 minutes. The game uses HTTP polling when the WebSocket is not available. The NASA API key lives only in the backend. If the live data fails, the game keeps working with saved data. A Supabase database is wired in but only activates with credentials. The shared sync is still in progress.

Super Intelligence tools used: Muse, a Meta AI assistant, and Claude, for code, architecture, and review of this submission.
